summary:
This evaluation covered 12 "ecr-guard" chat tasks testing an ECR lifecycle-policy guard agent, run with 1 iteration each (22 total runs). Two of the 12 evals were negative-trigger tests (should_trigger: false) and were correctly skipped for expected-output/assertions/metrics comparison in both variants — trigger_fired passed 100% for both on those.

Across the remaining 10 evals, with_skill and without_skill performed almost identically on most measured dimensions, and in several cases the results reveal weaknesses in the task/assertion design itself rather than differences between variants:

- Expected-output pass rate: both variants failed the overall expected-output check in most evals (e.g., ecr-guard-gap-h1-exact-list, h2-safe-to-leave, account-sweep, draft-policy-preview, production-tag-catch-all, unexpected-deletion-postmortem all show 0/1 for both, high confidence). Two evals diverged: "evaluation-v230-in-use" and "evaluation-cloudtrail-consumer-pull-in-use" had with_skill fail (0/1) while without_skill passed (1/1), and "evaluation-push-correlated-event-excluded" had both pass (1/1). These few passing cases used medium/high confidence judgments.
- Assertion-level pass rates were tied exactly in most evals (e.g., 2/11 and 2/11 on gap-h1-exact-list, 2/9 and 2/9 on h2-safe-to-leave, 1/8 and 1/8 on account-sweep, 1/7 and 1/7 on draft-policy-preview, 1/6 and 1/6 on production-tag-catch-all), with many "always_fails" patterns shared by both variants — indicating these specific behaviors (full-report formatting, required headings, SIMULATED/AUTHORITATIVE labeling, Check Matrix completeness, Repository Rating vocabulary) were not reliably produced by either variant, suggesting the underlying capability or the assertion criteria need attention rather than a variant-specific gap.
- Some per-assertion splits did appear: in "evaluation-five-rule-expiry-list" with_skill passed the "rc images mentioned as survivors" assertion while without_skill failed it (6/10 vs 5/10 overall). In "evaluation-v230-in-use" with_skill correctly cited the InUse evidence for v2.3.0 while without_skill did not (7/13 vs 6/13 overall). In "evaluation-push-correlated-event-excluded" the two variants split oppositely on two different assertions (with_skill correctly verdicted build-41 as Expiring-Unused while without_skill did not; without_skill correctly explained the push-correlation exclusion while with_skill did not), netting an identical 4/10 overall for both. In "evaluation-cloudtrail-consumer-pull-in-use" both tied at 5/10 with no assertion-level differences.
- Several assertions passed for both variants consistently (e.g., "no write API called," "image not called safe/unused when it shouldn't be"), confirming baseline safety behavior is solid for both and these assertions don't differentiate them.
- Runtime and cost: with_skill was generally faster and cheaper on the "gap" and "account-sweep" evals (e.g., 26s/$0.22 vs 49s/$0.41; 37s/$0.31 vs 57s/$0.48; 29s/$0.24 vs 43s/$0.36), while without_skill was faster/cheaper on "draft-policy-preview" (37s/$0.31 vs 53s/$0.45) and "production-tag-catch-all" (25s/$0.21 vs 38s/$0.32). So the runtime/cost advantage is not consistently one-sided. Several later evals show 0s/$0.00 for both, likely indicating no fresh run metrics were captured for those cases.
- Quality-comparison pairs were skipped in every eval (pairs_evaluated: 0, pairs_skipped: 1 throughout), so no direct pairwise quality judgment is available for any task.
- Output consistency (run-to-run) is null for both variants in all evals, since this run used 1 iteration per eval, so consistency cannot be assessed from this data.
- The "ecr-guard-unexpected-deletion-postmortem" eval has fully inconclusive/null assertion data for both variants, meaning no measurement could be made there at all.

Overall, this run shows very high similarity between with_skill and without_skill on expected-output and assertion outcomes for most tasks, with both sharing the same structural shortfalls (missing report sections, missing SIMULATED/AUTHORITATIVE labeling, missing Check Matrix detail) on many evals — suggesting these are shared gaps rather than one variant being deficient. Where differences appeared, they were small, assertion-specific, and did not consistently favor one variant: without_skill edged ahead on two expected-output checks and one push-correlation assertion, while with_skill edged ahead on an InUse-evidence assertion and a survivors-listing assertion. Timing/cost differences existed but swapped direction across evals, so neither variant was uniformly faster or cheaper. No quality-comparison or consistency data was available to weigh further, and some evals had very low signal (null or inconclusive) due to skip conditions or missing run data.

ecr-guard-gap-h1-exact-list.summary:
Both variants were run on a single chat-task eval (ECS lifecycle-policy / image-expiry reporting scenario), and the results are essentially identical between them on every measured dimension.

- Trigger/expected output: the trigger behavior under test did not fire (0/1), and both without_skill and with_skill failed to meet the expected output (0/1 each), with high confidence in that judgment. This indicates the underlying task/behavior itself did not succeed for either variant, rather than one variant being worse than the other.

- Assertions: both variants scored identically, 2/11 (18%) passing. Looking at the per-assertion breakdown, the same two assertions passed for both ("does not state any expiring image is safe/not a concern outside a verdict row" and "no write API reported as called") and the same nine assertions failed for both (e.g., full report vs. prose summary, AUTHORITATIVE/SIMULATED labeling, verdict-per-image with evidence, required section headings, Repository Rating values, Check Matrix rows, etc.). Every assertion pattern is "always_fails" or "always_passes" across both variants — none of the 11 assertions differentiate without_skill from with_skill. This points to systematic gaps in the underlying behavior/report structure common to both, not a difference between the two agents.

- Metrics: without_skill ran slower (~49s vs ~26s, about 23s longer) and cost more (~$0.41 vs ~$0.22, roughly double) than with_skill. Context window utilization was identical (3.7%, no compaction) for both. Since output correctness was equally poor for both variants, this runtime/cost difference isn't offset by any quality advantage for without_skill in this run — it's a plain cost/runtime difference without an accompanying quality tradeoff visible in the data.

- Quality comparison: no comparable pairs were evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no direct quality-preference signal between the two outputs.

- Output consistency: not available for either variant (null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall, this is a single-eval, single-run comparison where both variants failed the expected output and passed the same minority of assertions, with no assertion showing a split result. The main observed difference is without_skill's higher runtime and cost relative to with_skill, but since neither variant produced a passing or differentiated-quality output, this should be read as a shared shortfall in the behavior being tested rather than evidence that one variant outperforms the other. Confidence in the expected-output judgments is high, but the assertion failures (missing report structure, headings, verdicts) suggest the core capability being tested needs further work for both variants.

ecr-guard-gap-h2-safe-to-leave.summary:
Both variants were run on a single chat task and produced identical results on essentially every measured dimension, so this evaluation shows no meaningful difference between them.

- Trigger/expected output: The overall trigger behavior did not fire (0/1), and both without_skill and with_skill failed to meet the expected output (0/1 each), with high-confidence judgments on both sides — so this is a consistent, high-confidence finding that neither variant produced the expected result, not a case of weak measurement.

- Assertions: Both variants scored identically, 2/9 (22%) passed. Looking at the per-assertion breakdown, there is no case where one variant passed and the other failed — every assertion either passed for both or failed for both:
  - Passed by both: "does not end with an offer to modify/delete/investigate further" and "no write API reported as called."
  - Failed by both (all with high confidence, i.e. not a measurement artifact): the full structured report format, the lastRecordedPullTime evidence explanation, the EC2-pull/CloudTrail/24h-lag explanation, correct handling of AccessDenied on batch:DescribeJobDefinitions, and the protective lifecycle rule JSON requirement; and on the regex side, both the Repository Rating fixed-value check and the fixed verdict vocabulary check failed for both variants.
  - This pattern suggests the underlying task behavior itself (producing the full structured report with correct verdicts and explanations) is not being met by either variant, rather than one variant underperforming relative to the other.

- Quality comparison: No quality pairs could be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no data on relative output quality between the variants for this task.

- Runtime and cost: without_skill took ~57s and cost ~$0.48, while with_skill took ~37s and cost ~$0.31 — with_skill was faster and cheaper by about 20s and $0.17. Since quality could not be compared and assertion outcomes were identical, this runtime/cost difference is a standalone observation rather than a tradeoff against quality.

- Context window utilization was identical for both (3.7%, 0 compactions).

- Output consistency: No consistency data is available for either variant (both null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, this is a single-task, low-signal comparison: the two variants behaved identically on the pass/fail outcomes for every assertion and on the expected-output check, with no quality comparison possible. The only differentiating data point is that with_skill ran faster and cheaper than without_skill, but since both failed the same assertions, this does not establish one as more effective — it simply reflects a cost/runtime difference on this single run.

- Five LLM-graded assertions (about the Account Summary table, repository ordering, handling of repos without lifecycle policies, per-repository detail sections, and reporting of the in-use inventory collection) failed for both variants ("always_fails" pattern), all with high-confidence judgments. This indicates a consistent, confidently-measured gap in the expected behavior that applies equally to both variants rather than differentiating them.
- Two regex-based assertions (presence of an "Account Summary" heading, use of rating vocabulary) also failed for both variants.
- One regex assertion ("no write API reported as called") passed for both variants (100%), which is a check that both satisfy but doesn't differentiate them.
No assertion shows a split result where one variant passed and the other failed — the two variants are fully aligned on every individual check in this eval.

Context window utilization was nearly identical (3.9% vs 3.8%, no compactions for either). These are the only dimensions showing any difference, and since quality/output outcomes were identical (both failing the same assertions), the runtime/cost difference is a plain cost/speed distinction rather than a quality tradeoff.

Quality comparison and consistency: No quality pairs were actually evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no direct head-to-head quality judgment available. Output consistency across repeated runs is not available for either variant (null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall: this is a case where both variants behaved the same way on every assertion that was checked, and both failed the expected output for the task — indicating a likely gap in the behavior or task setup itself rather than a difference between the two variants. The only distinguishing data points are with_skill's lower runtime and cost. No quality or consistency comparison could be drawn due to skipped/unavailable data.

ecr-guard-evaluation-v230-in-use.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about assessing ECR image expiration/usage status for an ECS-related repository. The data available is thin (one task instance, no repeated runs), so confidence in any pattern here is limited.

Trigger and expected output: The `trigger_fired` check (0/1) did not fire, meaning the specific behavior being tested did not occur in this run — this is a measurement about the test setup itself, not a variant score. On the "expected_output" check, without_skill passed (1/1, medium confidence) while with_skill failed (0/1). This is a meaningful difference, but it rests on only one trial and medium-confidence judging, so it should be treated as a single data point rather than a robust trend.

Assertions (13 total per variant): Overall pass rates were close — with_skill passed 7/13 (54%) and without_skill passed 6/13 (46%). Breaking this down:
- 6 assertions passed for both variants (always_passes): no image called "Expiring-Unused," a protective tagPatternList rule present, v2.3.0 not called safe, no write API reported, the AtRisk rating/deciding-rule statement, and the "never describes v2.3.0 as safe" check. These are not differentiating — both variants satisfy them.
- 4 assertions failed for both variants (always_fails): the detailed "Expiring-Unknown" labeling for the batch AccessDenied case, the specific protective-rule JSON formatting requirement, the Batch/CloudTrail "Not Assessed/NotChecked" table presentation, and the regex check for "Expiring-Unknown ... Batch denied." These represent capability gaps or overly strict assertions that neither variant satisfies, suggesting either a genuine shared weakness or an assertion that may need review.
- 1 assertion showed a split result: "v2.3.0 is given verdict Expiring-InUse with lastRecordedPullTime cited as evidence" — with_skill passed (high confidence) and without_skill failed (medium confidence).
